title: Australia’s inflation test is persistence at capacity
summary: Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser considered a further near-term rate cut unlikely on the information available on 8 January. Inflation exceeded the top of the 2–3% target band, demand had recovered broadly as expected and businesses reported unusually high capacity utilisation for this stage of the cycle. Yet his interview gave no threshold for a February increase. The Board needed to decide whether the recent price acceleration reflected discounts unwinding as demand normalised or a more persistent encounter with supply constraints. Those explanations imply different inflation paths one to two years ahead, even when they generate the same quarterly reading today (opening exchanges and discussion of December-quarter inflation).

Australia had raised rates less than some peers during the post-pandemic inflation surge and cut three times in 2025 as disinflation progressed. Recent data weakened the case for continuing that earlier easing. November’s monthly CPI ticked down broadly as expected. Black Friday discounts helped durable goods, and market-services inflation was somewhat softer. New dwellings and rents pointed the other way. The monthly series was new enough for the Bank to be cautious about its interpretation. Hauser wanted the full December-quarter release and the next labour-market reading before revisiting the forecast. He thought underlying inflation in the December quarter might be marginally above the November forecast, without prejudging the February projections (exchanges on November CPI and the quarterly print).

The November forecast had inflation above 3% through late 2025 and into early 2026 before it moved gradually back to just above the 2.5% midpoint. That projection assumed rates would fall. A lower likelihood of a cut would itself affect the conditioning assumptions when the forecast was redone. Hauser stressed the difference between a rise in the price level that temporarily lifts annual inflation and a shortage of productive capacity that keeps underlying inflation high. Business evidence on utilisation raised the probability of the latter explanation, without settling the issue. Even a very large CPI surprise would require an explanation of its composition and durability. He explicitly rejected the idea that a few tenths of a percentage point on the quarterly number could mechanically decide between a hold, hike or cut.

Easing later in 2026 remained conceivable under two very different scenarios. A global shock or abrupt labour-market weakening could force cuts into a downturn. Alternatively, the productive capacity of the economy could prove greater than the Bank had assumed. Australia could then sustain stronger activity with less inflation, making a cut compatible with good growth. Some market participants saw merit in the supply scenario; Hauser said it was outside the Bank’s central case. The interviewer cited roughly a one-third probability of a February increase and about two increases priced by year-end. Hauser thought the pricing somewhat lower and declined to endorse the February odds. This distinction matters for an event study: the probability came from the interviewer’s account of the market, while the policy signal concerned the low likelihood of an imminent cut (early exchanges on rates pricing).

Variable-rate mortgages transmit a change in policy quickly to Australian borrowers’ servicing costs. Hauser nevertheless saw little basis for inferring the economy’s overall interest sensitivity from mortgages alone. He pointed to exchange rates, business pricing and credit, and distinguished aggregate household balance sheets, which had benefited from pandemic-era rebuilding and substantial assets, from the immediate cash demands on indebted households. APRA’s lending restrictions were preventative in his account: they could restrain future investor borrowing if credit accelerated, even if they did little to change existing lending on the day. Low confidence despite relatively low unemployment and improved inflation could reflect households’ experience of the earlier price increases (exchanges on housing, leverage and confidence).

International developments supplied upside as well as downside risks. Tariffs had been narrower, retaliation less extensive and supply chains more adaptable than feared. Policy stimulus and the technology investment cycle supported Asian suppliers of memory chips and servers. In the opposite direction, geopolitical flashpoints or a sharp correction from high technology valuations could hurt Australia. Hauser used Venezuelan oil as an illustration of the difference between an announcement and a physical supply response: more output could eventually reduce Australian fuel costs, but he saw little contemporaneous oil-price effect. The interview offered scenarios for demand and inflation, with no measured exchange-rate or asset-price response attributed to his remarks (closing exchanges on the global outlook).

questions.question: How much of the December-quarter underlying inflation surprise would be expected to persist?
questions.detail: Hauser identifies discount reversals, housing costs and capacity pressure, but does not quantify their contributions. The distinction determines whether a strong print changes the one-to-two-year inflation outlook that matters for policy. Compare the quarterly component breakdown against the November RBA forecasts and the monthly release. Look for broader and repeated price increases in capacity-constrained sectors, while checking the timing of seasonal discounts and new-dwelling price changes.

questions.question: Could evidence of greater supply capacity make a cut compatible with strong activity?
questions.detail: The interview gives this interpretation some weight while keeping it outside the central case. It matters because a decline in short yields would have different implications for earnings and the currency under favourable supply news and a demand shock. Compare the business-capacity survey Hauser cites with productivity, hours, employment and wage data available ahead of the February meeting. Test whether stronger output is being delivered without rising unit costs.

questions.question: Whose consumption changes first when variable mortgage payments rise?
questions.detail: The aggregate balance sheet described by Hauser gives little information on the overlap between mortgage debt, liquid savings and household income. That overlap matters for the timing of monetary transmission and any bank-credit exposure. The RBA’s financial stability review, referred to in the interview, is a starting point. Household-level servicing burdens, redraw or offset balances and spending by mortgage vintage would help distinguish a rapid cash-flow shock from an aggregate wealth effect.
